 Live .  6,617 viewing 6617 viewing Live page Updated 9 minutes ago Bomb hoaxes across Europe disrupt flights as two UK airports also receive threats
 Summary
 At least 21 flights across Europe have been impacted by bomb threats - a list of what journeys we know have been affected 
 It comes days after seven flights were affected by similar threats 
 Both London Heathrow and Birmingham Airports say they received threats earlier on Thursday , with Heathrow saying its was "deemed not credible" 
 Airport authorities in Rome say they received one via email from a group called "Fighters of the Male State" , claiming to be targeting a "feminist regime"
 That name likely refers to the Russian group Muzhskoi Legion, our security correspondent Frank Gardener writes - but even if the email is genuine it is unlikely to provide the leads to track down who is generating these hoaxes 
 An Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome was diverted to a French military air base - one passenger tells the BBC "we were all trying to be as calm as we could" 
 Meanwhile, military fighter jets escorted one plane into Rome Fiumicino Airport and three aircraft to airports in Sofia

 Edited by Jamie Whitehead and Matt Spivey
 Aer Lingus pilot 'being investigated by French prosecutors' published at 18:17 GMT 18:17 GMT 
 The pilot of the Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome,
which was diverted to France's Évreux-Fauvill Air Base, is reportedly being
investigated by French prosecutors.
 Évreux prosecutor Remi Coutin said he was told the pilot had
refused to land at the military base, preferring a civilian airport instead,
before two fighter jets were sent to escort the plane, according to both the AFP
and Reuters news agencies.
 Coutin said he will probe whether the pilot refused to
comply with the request to land and if such a refusal could be a criminal offence,
Reuters added.
 Earlier, Aer Lingus said the flight, which departed Dublin at 06:40 GMT, was diverted to Normandy "as a safety precaution" and "landed safely".

 Pilot told us we were targeted with same threat as we'd seen on the news, passenger tells BBC published at 17:47 GMT 17:47 GMT 
 Kris Bramwell 
BBC News 
 Image source, Supplied Image caption, Luke Pearson says his plane was surrounded by fire crews before being told to disembark
 A passenger who was on board a Barcelona-bound plane waiting to take off at Birmingham Airport this morning had to wait "about an hour and a half" before swapping onto a new aircraft.
 Luke Pearson, 26, says the captain told passengers that they were "targeted with the same threats that 'we have likely seen on recent news'".
 After returning to the gate in the airport, he says passengers were "surrounded by fire crews and safety cars". Pearson says he was able to go back through security and board a new flight "with no further issues".
 Jet2, the airline operating the flight, tells the BBC checks were carried out on the plane and passengers were transferred to a replacement aircraft following a "security precaution".
 The airline adds that nothing was found following the search.
 Earlier, a Birmingham Airport spokesperson told the BBC it had received a threat, after which "processes were immediately initiated in conjunction with emergency services and partners".

 International Air Transport Association urges authorities to 'find the origins of hoax threats' published at 17:34 GMT 17:34 GMT 
 The International Air Transport Association (IATA) has urged
authorities to "find the origins" of the "hoax threats"
targeting flights across Europe this week.
 "We condemn these attempts to disrupt air
transport," IATA senior vice president for operations safety and security
Nick Careen says in a statement, adding that "safety is a number one
priority for the industry".
 "Meanwhile passengers should be assured that aviation
security measures will continue to ensure the highest levels of public
safety," he adds.

 Tough to pin down who is behind hoaxes - but some are pointing finger at Russia published at 17:17 GMT 17:17 GMT 
 Frank Gardner 
Security correspondent 
 It is hardly surprising that the simultaneous, coordinated
nature of these airline hoaxes - coupled with other malicious actions across
Europe such as the remote hacking of supermarket freezers and an incident on
Poland’s border with Russia - are causing some to point the finger of suspicion
at Russia.
 This is surely, they argue, another example of Russian
hybrid warfare aimed at punishing Nato countries for their support for Ukraine.
 And it could be, we just don’t know yet.
 As of mid-afternoon on Thursday no hard evidence had emerged
linking the airline hoaxes to Moscow or any proxy groups controlled by the
Kremlin.
 There is the threat email sent this morning to airport
authorities in Rome, purporting to be from “Fighters of the Male State”.
 That name likely refers to the Russian group Muzhskoi Legion
or “Male Legion,” an ultra-right group with such extreme views it was banned by
a Moscow court in 2021.
 Yet it retained tens of thousands of online followers as it
cheered on the subsequent full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine.
 But that email, even if genuine, is unlikely to provide the
leads that police and airport authorities need to pin down who is generating
these hoaxes and why.

 Four key things a fighter pilot does when jets are scrambled to escort aircraft published at 17:05 GMT 17:05 GMT 
 By Charlotte Green 
 Several flights targeted by bomb threats were escorted to
land by fighter jets this morning.
 Marco Chan, senior lecturer in aviation operations at
Kingston University and former Cathay Pacific pilot, says escorts are scrambled
on the orders of military, regardless of the credibility of the threat, as they
are the "only force that can put a pilot beside the aircraft within
minutes".
 He says the fighter pilot’s role is to:
 Inspect the outside of the aircraft and confirm it behaves as the crew reports
 Guide it to the designated airfield, away from populated areas, with a way to communicate if radio fails
 Relay what they see to the military on the ground
 Reassure the crew and passengers, plus stay in position if the situation escalates
 Chan adds that escorts are not put in place to "shoot down a threatened airliner".

 How do countries respond to aircraft posing a threat? published at 16:50 GMT 16:50 GMT 
 Rich Preston 
BBC News 
 Nato has an "air policing'" plan as part of its
procedures to protect European members' airspace.
 If an aircraft is suspicious, unidentified, or has issued a
distress signal, it is reported to a Nato Air Operations Centre, where a
decision is made on whether or not to scramble a Quick Reaction Alert (QRA)
Interceptor aircraft - in other words, a fighter jet.
 These are aircraft and pilots which are on standby 24/7.
 If launched, QRA jets will approach the suspicious plane and
attempt to make visual and radio contact with the pilot.
 Depending on the circumstances, they will then fly alongside
the plane and escort it either to a nearby airbase, or out of Nato airspace.
 Nato says its radars monitor 35,000 air movements per day,
and whilst most scenarios in which QRA planes are scrambled are harmless, Nato
has to always assume the worst.
 In our next post, we'll take a closer look at the job of the fighter pilot when escorting aircraft.

 Air travel chaos as at least 21 flights impacted by reported threats published at 16:27 GMT 16:27 GMT 
 Jack Grey 
Live reporter 
 So far today at least 21 flights have reportedly been
impacted amid a wave of suspected hoax bomb threats across Europe.
 It follows similar disruption earlier in the week, when at least seven flights were
searched across Europe following a series of bomb threats.
 Impacted airlines include:
 Aegean - Two flights received threats, both arrived at destination
 Aer
 Lingus - Dublin to Rome diverted to France's Évreux-Fauvill
 airbase
 Air
 Europa - Madrid to Paris Orly flight evacuated before take-off but
 later cleared for departure
 Air Serbia - Belgrade to Bucharest received a threat after take-off, arrived at destination
 Easyjet - Two flights to Prague affected, arrived at destination
 Finnair - Two outbound flights from Helsinki subjected to threats, arrived at destinations
 Iberia - Two flights to Madrid impacted, arrived at destination
 LOT - Warsaw to Paris flight stopped before take off, second flight to Brussels arrived at destination
 Ryanair - Four flights subjected to threats - with London Stansted to Sofia diverted to Plovdiv
 Wizz Air - Two flights affected, with Milan to Warsaw diverted to Vienna 
 Czech police also say bomb threats were received on four
flights to Prague , all of which landed in the Czech capital with no
explosives found - it is not clear if this includes the two Easyjet flights
reported above.
 London Heathrow and Birmingham airports have also both reported
receiving "threats" on Thursday .
 There has been no confirmation that any explosives have been
found follow any of the reported threats.

 Aer Lingus passengers tried to ‘be as calm as we could’ published at 16:03 GMT 16:03 GMT 
 Image source, Emily Noble Image caption, Emily Noble is waiting for a transfer to Rome at an air base in France
 By Emma Pengelly 
 Emily Noble says she was about an hour into her flight to
Rome to attend a friend’s wedding when passengers were told about a “technical”
problem.
 Later, as the Aer Lingus plane began circling for an
unplanned landing in France, the pilot said there was a “security” issue, the
26-year-old from Dublin tells BBC Verify.
 On board it was “an odd experience,” Noble says. “It was
worrying because we didn’t know what was going on, but we were all trying to be
as calm as we could.”
 Noble says she could hear fighter jets during the landing
and saw one touch down behind the plane she was on. 
 After landing at the Évreux-Fauville military air base in
Normandy, passengers learned the flight had been the subject of a bomb threat.
 They remained on board for over two hours while police and
military personnel carried out checks, Noble says, including searches with
sniffer dogs.
 The passengers have been told they will be taken to an
airport in Paris and another plane will fly them on to Rome.

 Air Serbia flight security threat 'assessed as unfounded' after landing in Romania published at 15:38 GMT 15:38 GMT 
 More now on the Air Serbia flight from Belgrade to Bucharest, which we reported on earlier. 
 The airline has confirmed a bomb threat was reported to
authorities at Bucharest Airport after the flight had left the Serbian capital.
 The aircraft arrived safely at its destination, where
Romanian authorities "carried out procedures in accordance with applicable
security protocols" and "the security threat was assessed as
unfounded", it adds in a statement.
 The aircraft has been returned to regular operational
service, Air Serbia adds.

 Heathrow and Birmingham airports say they received 'threats' today published at 15:26 GMT 15:26 GMT 
 Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Passengers outside London's Heathrow Airport after an air traffic control failure in September
 London Heathrow Airport and Birmingham Airport both say they
received "threats" earlier today.
 Heathrow says in a statement that it received a threat
earlier today which was "deemed not credible", adding there was no
risk to passengers, colleagues or the aircraft.
 “There are robust UK aviation security standards in place to
assess and safely manage these types of situations,” it said. 
 Meanwhile a Birmingham Airport spokesperson tells the BBC
that it received a threat, after which "processes were immediately
initiated in conjunction with emergency services and partners".

 Air Serbia says flight from Belgrade to Bucharest received bomb threat published at 15:02 GMT 15:02 GMT 
 Image source, AFP via Getty Images An Air Serbia plane flying from Belgrade to Bucharest
received a bomb threat before safely landing in its intended destination, the
country’s national air carrier says in a statement seen by the Reuters news
agency.

 Iberia Airlines says two of its flights received 'explosive' threats published at 14:49 GMT 14:49 GMT 
 Image source, Getty Images Iberia Airlines says two of its aircraft received "explosive threats" this morning, adding that these turned out to be "false alarms". 
 These warnings were sent to Madrid-Barajas Airport, it says in a statement.
 The airline says these messages were then relayed to the pilots of both flights, which went to land in Madrid at approximately 10:00 local time (09:00 GMT).
 "Passengers disembarked without any problems, in accordance with established security protocols," it says. 
 The affected flights where IBE668 from Milan to Madrid, and IBE658 from Rome to Madrid.

 Aegean confirms two of its flights received bomb threats published at 14:35 GMT 14:35 GMT 
 Nikos Papanikolaou 
BBC News 
 Two Aegean Airlines flights were targeted by bomb threats on Thursday, the Greek carrier has confirmed.
 The threats concerned flight A3552 from Thessaloniki to Milan, which we reported on earlier , and flight A3860 from Athens to Vienna. Both aircraft landed safely at their destinations.
 Greece’s Deputy Foreign Minister, Tasos Chatzivassiliou, was among the passengers on the Vienna-bound flight.
 In a statement, Aegean said it had worked closely with the relevant authorities and followed all required security procedures before the flights departed, after the threats were found to be unfounded.

 Fighter jets accompanied affected flights in Austrian airspace - defence ministry published at 14:30 GMT 14:30 GMT 
 Austria's defence ministry says fighter jets were deployed to assist all affected flights in Austrian airspace. 
 "Due to bomb threats against civilian aircraft, all affected flights in Austrian airspace were escorted by Eurofighters," spokesperson Michael Bauer writes in a post on X. 
 Italy has confirmed fighter jets were used to escort a flight into Rome airport earlier, while Bulgaria also used jets to escort flights.

 EasyJet says two UK-Prague flights met by police as precaution published at 14:21 GMT 14:21 GMT 
 EasyJet says two of its flights, one from Newcastle and one from Glasgow, were met by police after arriving in Prague as a "precautionary measure" due to a "security related matter".
 "Passengers on both flights disembarked normally," the airline says.
 Earlier, Czech police said four flights were inspected after arriving in Prague due to bomb threats, but that no explosives were found.
 Local Czech media has since reported that two of these flights had departed from the UK.

 Threats reported in 'early hours' have been 'resolved' - UK government published at 14:10 GMT 14:10 GMT 
 A UK government spokesperson says the threats reported in the "early hours" of Thursday - described by the transport secretary earlier as "malicious hoaxes" - have been "resolved".
 In a statement the spokesperson says it is "right that authorities treat any potential threats seriously" and that the UK has "one of the most robust aviation security systems in the world".
 "The Met’s Aviation Policing Command continues to monitor the situation and liaise with the relevant authorities," it adds.

 Airlines receive bomb threats every day, but this is different - aviation expert published at 13:58 GMT 13:58 GMT 
 Gabriela Pomeroy 
Live reporter 
 Image source, Philip Baum The aviation industry "faces multiple bomb threats every single day", says Philip Baum, professor of aviation security at the University of Coventry.
 But he is "surprised" at this week's incidents, which are "different as the threats have been classified by the authorities as specific".
 That does not mean that every aircraft subject to a threat is diverted, he says. 
 A flight is diverted "only when the threat is credible and the authorities believe - from the source or nature of the threat - that there is a potential of an explosive device on board."
 Baum adds that "most people who put bombs on planes to do not tell people about it before - they claim it after the event".
 But the concern is that "if you issue enough hoax threats, then complacency could set in and a real threat could be ignored - or they could be a diversion".

 Dublin Airport 'operating as normal' after flight bound for Rome diverted published at 13:56 GMT 13:56 GMT 
 Dublin airport is "operating as normal" after an Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome was diverted to a French military base near Paris following a bomb threat, according to a spokesperson. 
 "We have about 70,000 passengers going through, about 600 flights coming in and out, so it’s very much a normal day, passengers should continue to travel, arrive to the airport as normal, and expect to make your flight," Graeme McQueen, head of communications with Dublin Airport operator daa says.
 He adds that a flight leaving Dublin Airport for Rome this morning "did divert to an airport in Paris", but "other than that, it’s a normal day" and "people getting on their way" at the airport.

 At least 18 flights reportedly impacted by threats published at 13:31 GMT 13:31 GMT 
 Jack Grey 
Live reporter 
 Image source, Reuters Image caption, Passengers have disembarked an Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome which was diverted to a French air base
 So far today there have been at least 18 flights reportedly impacted by bomb threats across Europe.
 They are:
 Aegean Thessaloniki to Milan , landed in Milan
 Aer Lingus Dublin to Rome , diverted to France's Evreux airbase
 Finnair Helsinki to Rome , landed in Rome
 Finnair Helsinki to Vienna , landed in Vienna
 Wizz Air Milan to Bucharest , landed in Bucharest
 Wizz Air Milan to Warsaw , diverted to Vienna
 LOT Warsaw to Brussels , landed in Brussels
 LOT Warsaw to Paris , stopped before take-off 
 Ryanair Porto to Milan , landed in Milan
 Ryanair Copenhagen to Sofia , landed in Sofia 
 Ryanair Madrid to Sofia , landed in Sofia
 Ryanair London Stansted to Sofia, diverted to Plovdiv
 Czech police also say bomb threats were received on four flights to Prague , all of which landed in Prague with no explosives found - local media reports these four flights departed from Greece, Ireland and two from the UK. 
 Spain's airport authority says it received bomb threats affecting three flights at Madrid airport on Thursday, but that any threat was ruled out following inspections - it is not yet clear if this includes the above reported Ryanair Madrid to Sofia flight.
 As we've been reporting, UK Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander says flights across the continent have been hit by "malicious hoax threats" which the EU transport chief says authorities are investigating .

 Watch: Passengers depart plane in Warsaw after security threat published at 13:19 GMT 13:19 GMT 
 Media caption, Watch: Passengers depart plane in Warsaw after bomb threat
 An eyewitness video shows passengers evacuating a flight from Warsaw to Paris after reports of a "potential security threat". 
 "Take-off aborted on the runway. Police, military and sniffer dogs met us. All passengers evacuated to a separate hall," the eyewitness, @bibibebaboy, wrote on X.
 As we've just reported, LOT Polish Airlines says the plane was stopped while taxiing and directed to a designated parking stand after reports of a "potential security threat", before undergoing a security screening from authorities.
 No hazardous items were found, it says, and passengers will continue their journey on a different aircraft.
